summary: Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) safety copilot trained on 393 real NASA ISS combustion runs (FLEX, BASS-II, and SAME). In microgravity, buoyancy disappears and smoke drifts sideways rather than rising, delaying traditional ceiling alarms while invisible cool flames and elevated oxygen levels create flashover and carbon monoxide hazards. Flame in Freefall summarizes decades of NASA orbital combustion telemetry, ranks live cabin fire risk on a 100-point severity index, and recommends targeted suppression actions—achieving 89.87% 5-fold cross-validation accuracy and zero missed critical fires (0/40) on unseen test data.
details:
Live Interactive App: https://flame-in-freefall-nasa.streamlit.app/

Source Code and Data Repository (GitHub): https://github.com/Prasiddha976/flame-in-freefall

THE PROBLEM

On Earth, thermal buoyancy lifts hot combustion gases upward into ceiling smoke detectors. In microgravity, natural convection disappears. Smoke drifts sideways with cabin ventilation instead of rising, delaying standard ceiling alarms by critical minutes. Meanwhile, spherical diffusion flames and low-temperature cool flames can burn with minimal visible light while generating lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide. Enriched-oxygen exploration atmospheres planned for Lunar Gateway, Artemis habitats, and Mars transit vehicles further elevate flashover risk.

THE SOLUTION

Flame in Freefall is a real-time predictive fire safety dashboard designed for spacecraft ECLSS monitoring, built from scratch as a solo Class 9 student project. Rather than relying solely on delayed smoke detection, the system evaluates cabin atmosphere chemistry, fuel geometry, and trace gas readings to predict fire severity and radiative self-extinction windows before flashover occurs.

KEY CAPABILITIES

1. Real-Time ECLSS Telemetry Deck: Operators can adjust cabin pressure, oxygen percentage, helium diluent percentage, carbon monoxide concentration, and fuel diameter, or test four benchmark mission scenarios (Nominal ISS, 26% O2 Flashover Hazard, Invisible Wire Smoldering, and 35% Helium Inert Quench).

2. Physics-Informed Machine Learning: The preprocessing pipeline derives thermodynamic and kinetic invariants from NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) telemetry, including oxygen partial pressure (Dalton's Law), gas mixture thermal conductivity across helium, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and oxygen, D2-law kinematic residence timescales, and toxic smoldering ratios.

3. Actionable Suppression Directives: Generates immediate crew and automated ECLSS responses, including ventilation throttling, electrical bus isolation, and inert gas injection.

4. Interactive 3D Combustion Phase Space: Visualizes live cabin conditions directly against 393 historical NASA ISS experiments alongside an embedded Model Validation and Safety Audit tab.

VERIFIED PERFORMANCE

- Dataset: 393 real NASA ISS experimental runs spanning liquid droplets, solid polymers, fabrics, and wire insulation.

- Fire Risk Classifier (5-Fold Cross-Validation): 89.87% accuracy across SAFE, WARNING, and CRITICAL regimes.

- Critical Fire Recall (Holdout): 95.0% sensitivity to flashover and toxic smoldering hazards.

- Catastrophic False Negatives: 0 out of 40 Critical fires misclassified as Safe on unseen test runs.

- Extinction Time Regressor: R2 of 0.76 with 2.50 seconds mean absolute error.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

Artificial intelligence and machine learning form the core analytical engine of Flame in Freefall. Using Python, Scikit-learn, and XGBoost, I trained two supervised models on 393 real NASA ISS combustion runs: a multi-class Fire Risk Classifier that categorizes cabin hazards into SAFE, WARNING, or CRITICAL regimes in real time (89.87% cross-validation accuracy and 0 out of 40 missed critical fires), and an Extinction Time Regressor that estimates the radiative self-extinction window in seconds (R2 of 0.76, 2.50s mean absolute error) to guide helium quenching and ventilation directives.

In addition, I used generative AI tools during development and media production: AI-generated cartoon character animation and AI text-to-speech narration for the 24-second project demo video, and AI coding assistants to debug code and draft documentation. All physics-informed feature engineering, data processing, model training, validation audits, and telemetry logic were designed and verified by me as a solo student developer.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

I thank NASA and the NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) team for making decades of International Space Station microgravity combustion research openly accessible to students and researchers worldwide. Specifically, this project relies on experimental data and foundational fire science from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX, PSI-69), the Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II, PSI-25), and the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME, PSI-102) principal investigators and flight teams. I also thank the NASA Space Apps Challenge global organizers and Universal Event leads for providing the platform for high school students worldwide to build open-source space safety tools.
